{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-sc-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"6f8e6acef0a261937a5065d7467d3227c8f5d7d8e141a037db03beac0f37e3da","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-sc-class-d:lineage:46","source_registry_sha256":"61c32f86a25e3c021742b3c9ddf64a97709817dd75a19df6d2b69eac0a40c4f1","source_liveness_sha256":"feb7871590284d2a19ab0509ff65b48154ba15e637a6ec9b839f55a72736ffdb"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Safe driving tips: visual search, speed management, stopping distance, space management and communicating","heading":"C — Visual search, adjusting speed for curves, wet roads and floods, the parts of stopping distance, the four-second following gap, side and rear space, and headlights, horn and signals","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Visual search, adjusting speed for curves, wet roads and floods, the parts of stopping distance, the four-second following gap, side and rear space, and headlights, horn and signals
Knowledge domain: the habits a South Carolina driver practices to stay safe, from where and how far to look, through slowing for curves, rain, hydroplaning and flooded roads, to what makes up stopping distance, how to keep a space cushion all around the vehicle, and how to use headlights, the horn, turn signals and brake lights to communicate.

FACT_ID: sec11-F01 | anchor: A01
Before starting the vehicle and while driving, you must know what is happening around you by looking ahead, to the sides and behind. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec11-F02 | anchor: A01
Develop a searching pattern for your eyes and use it every time you drive. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec11-F03 | anchor: A01
Searching shows you situations that could become a problem and gives you time to change your speed or road position, so keep your eyes moving instead of staring at any one thing. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec11-F04 | anchor: A01
Looking well down your planned path gives you time to adjust and plan, leads to better decisions and may spare you from emergency braking and steering. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec11-F05 | anchor: A01
Ideally, try to watch what is happening 20 to 30 seconds ahead of your vehicle. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec11-F06 | anchor: A02
Avoid situations that cut how far you can see, such as following a larger vehicle too closely, and adjust your speed and road position to see best. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec11-F07 | anchor: A02
Stay aware of traffic behind you, using your mirrors, especially when you change lanes, slow down or stop, or enter an intersection. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec11-F08 | anchor: A02
Driving safely means adjusting your speed to road and traffic conditions, keeping an adequate following distance and obeying the speed limits that apply. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec11-F09 | anchor: A02
Always slow down before you enter a curve, to a safe speed that lets you apply slight and constant acceleration all the way through it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec11-F10 | anchor: A02
Slow down even more on a curve when traction is poor, when you are following other vehicles and when you cannot see where the curve ends. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec11-F11 | anchor: A03
Reduce your speed at the first sign of rain, snow, sleet or ice. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec11-F12 | anchor: A03
On a slippery road your tires grip less, so stopping takes longer and turning without skidding is harder. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec11-F13 | anchor: A03
Hydroplaning is when your steering tires end up riding on a film of water above the road surface, much like water skis. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec11-F14 | anchor: A03
The best way to avoid losing traction to hydroplaning is to slow down in the rain or on roads with pooled water or puddles. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec11-F15 | anchor: A04
If you see a flooded road, or barricades blocking one, find another route to where you are going. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec11-F16 | anchor: A04
Flash floods can come quickly and without warning, within a few minutes or hours of excessive rainfall. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec11-F17 | anchor: A04
Six inches of water reaches the bottom of most passenger cars and can cause loss of control or stalling. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec11-F18 | anchor: A04
Two feet of moving water can sweep away most vehicles, including sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec11-F19 | anchor: A04
Never try to cross a flooded road even if it looks shallow, because the water can hide dips and other hazards and can wash away the road's underlying surface. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec11-F20 | anchor: A05
Total stopping distance is how far your vehicle travels, in ideal conditions, from the moment you realize you must stop until it actually stops. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec11-F21 | anchor: A05
The faster you are going, the more time and distance you need to stop. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec11-F22 | anchor: A05
Perception time is the time and distance it takes to recognize that you must stop, and for an alert driver it averages ¾ second to 1 second. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec11-F23 | anchor: A05
Reaction time is the time and distance it takes to move your foot from the gas pedal and start braking, and it averages ¾ second to 1 second. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec11-F24 | anchor: A05
Braking distance is the time and distance your brakes need to stop the vehicle, about 158 feet at 50 mph on dry pavement with good brakes. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec11-F25 | anchor: A05
The more space you leave between you and other road users, the more time you have to react; this space is called a space cushion, and you should keep one all around your vehicle. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec11-F26 | anchor: A05
Following the vehicle ahead too closely limits your view of the road and leaves too little time to react and avoid a collision. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec11-F27 | anchor: A06
Always try to keep a following distance of at least 4 seconds behind the vehicle in front. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec11-F28 | anchor: A06
To check the gap, note when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes a sign, pole or other fixed point, then count one thousand one, one thousand two and so on until you reach that point. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec11-F29 | anchor: A06
If you reach the fixed point before counting to one thousand four, you are too close, so slow down and count again at another point until the gap is at least 4 seconds. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec11-F30 | anchor: A06
Increase your following distance on slippery roads. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec11-F31 | anchor: A07
Also leave more room at night, in fog or bad weather, behind vehicles that must stop at railroad crossings such as transit buses, school buses and hazardous materials carriers, and behind large vehicles like trucks, buses, RVs and vehicles towing trailers. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec11-F32 | anchor: A07
Avoid driving beside other vehicles for long stretches, because you may sit in their blind spot and lose the side space you might need to avoid a crash. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec11-F33 | anchor: A07
Do not crowd the centerline, and keep as much room as you can between you and oncoming traffic. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec11-F34 | anchor: A08
Give pedestrians extra space, especially children, elderly people and bicyclists. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0100]

FACT_ID: sec11-F35 | anchor: A08
When a tractor trailer passes you, give it more room by moving to the outer part of your lane, away from the truck. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0100]

FACT_ID: sec11-F36 | anchor: A08
Headlights help others see you, especially on rainy, snowy or foggy days, when you should use low beams and slow down, and as it gets dark or when you drive away from a rising or setting sun. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0100]

FACT_ID: sec11-F37 | anchor: A09
A light horn tap is useful when pedestrians or bicyclists seem to be moving into your lane, when you pass a driver who starts turning into your lane, or when a driver is not paying attention or may not see you. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec11-F38 | anchor: A09
Use the horn only to communicate, since misuse can scare or anger other road users, and do not use it near blind pedestrians. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec11-F39 | anchor: A09
South Carolina law requires a turn signal at least 100 feet before you change lanes, turn left or right, or merge into traffic. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec11-F40 | anchor: A10
Brake lights tell others you are slowing, and you should signal before slowing when turning off a road that has no separate turn or exit lane, or when parking or turning just before an intersection. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0102]

Misconceptions: braking hard once you are already in a curve can cost traction, so the slowing happens before the curve; shallow-looking floodwater can still hide dips and wash out the road; total stopping distance includes the time to notice and react, not only braking; the four-second gap is a minimum, not a target, and grows in bad conditions; the horn is for communicating, not for venting anger.
Mnemonics: look twenty to thirty seconds ahead, follow at least four seconds behind; six inches stalls a car, two feet of moving water carries it away; perceive, react, then brake; signal one hundred feet before you move.
Glossary: visual search means a regular pattern of checking ahead, to the sides and behind; space cushion means the open space you keep around your vehicle; hydroplaning means tires riding on a film of water instead of the road; perception time means the time to recognize you must stop; reaction time means the time to move your foot to the brake; braking distance means the distance the brakes need to stop the vehicle; flash flood means a flood that arrives quickly after heavy rain.
